title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals used generative AI to create deepfakes and impersonate real people, including an immigration attorney in South Florida, to conduct fraud against victims in Georgia and Florida. The scammers cloned voices from social media, spoofed phone numbers, created fake photographs, and impersonated relatives in schemes targeting immigrants and others. This was a failure of identity verification at the point where victims encountered these fake personas, since no human confirmation process existed to validate whether they were communicating with genuine professionals or relatives.

The scams succeeded because victims had no way to authenticate the identities presenting themselves through voice calls and social media. Banks and law enforcement reported the scams were becoming harder to detect as the technology improved. To have caught these before they caused losses would have required victims to verify urgent requests through independent contact methods, but this depends on individual behavior rather than system design.

It is not established how the perpetrators obtained the original voice recordings used for cloning, or what specific generative AI tools or services they employed.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. In one case, a South Florida immigration attorney discovered scammers had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scheme. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia recorded 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers are using generative AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and impersonate relatives in grandparent scams and other fraud schemes. Banks like Truist are warning customers that these scams are becoming harder to detect. To protect themselves, people should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests by contacting people directly through known phone numbers, never send money based on phone calls alone, and report suspected scams to law enforcement. Investigators warn that as AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, these scams will likely continue evolving.
